idiom_name: java.util.ServiceLoader on the JVM (Kotlin interfaces and classes as providers)
implementation_notes: Kotlin compiles to JVM bytecode, so the JDK's ServiceLoader is the plugin mechanism unchanged: the contract is a Kotlin interface, providers are Kotlin classes with a public no-argument constructor listed in META-INF/services or declared with provides in module-info, and the host reads them with ServiceLoader.load(Formatter::class.java). Where the runtime is not the JVM there is no dynamic class loading at all - Kotlin/JS cannot reference ServiceLoader and Kotlin/Native links providers at build time - so a multi-platform host has to generate registration code at compile time or host extensions in a separate process. User-supplied behaviour that is written rather than prebuilt is better served by the Kotlin scripting API or a JSR-223 engine, which compiles a script against the published host API instead of loading a class.
code_sketch:
interface Formatter { fun format(doc: Document): String }

val loader: ServiceLoader<Formatter> = ServiceLoader.load(Formatter::class.java)
val available = loader.stream().map { it.type().name }.toList()   // no instantiation
val first = loader.first()
loader.reload()                                                   // new provider JARs
pitfalls: ServiceLoader.load resolves against the thread context class loader, so framework-style hosts that reset it (embedding engines, reloading engines) see an empty iterator instead of an error.
Kotlin object singletons are not no-argument-constructible for the loader (they are classes with a MODULE$ field), so a provider must be a class or use the static provider() factory hook.
Android's shrinking and packaging can strip or rename META-INF/services entries, which is why kotlinx.coroutines ships a hand-written service loader that falls back to Class.forName on Android.
